1. CSS SCROLL-DRIVEN ANIMATIONS (`animation-timeline: scroll()` and `view()`, `scroll-timeline`, `@keyframes` driven by scroll). Get the CURRENT browser support as of 2026 — check caniuse.com/css-scroll-driven-animations, MDN, and Chrome/WebKit/Mozilla release notes. Specifically: is it in Safari now (which version), Firefox (shipped or still behind a flag?), Chrome (since 115). Note that these run off-main-thread / composited — verify and cite. Note the `@supports (animation-timeline: scroll())` progressive-enhancement pattern.

2. SVG path/filter animation — feTurbulence + feDisplacementMap for aurora-like distortion, SMIL vs CSS vs JS, and the known PERFORMANCE cost of animating SVG filters (they're rasterized on CPU in many engines). Find real benchmarks/commentary.

3. CANVAS 2D — hand-rolled ribbon/perlin-noise aurora, cost, and how it handles DPR/retina and large viewports.

4. WebGL / Three.js / OGL / shader-based — bundle size of three.js (get the real current minified+gzip number), vs lighter options (OGL, twgl, raw WebGL, or a single full-screen fragment shader). Mention paper-shaders / Paper Design's shaders library if it exists, and any 2026 aurora-shader libraries. Note WebGL context cost on low-end mobile, battery, and the "heavy 3D runtime" concern.

5. VIDEO / IMAGE-SEQUENCE SCRUBBING — scroll-scrubbed video (the Apple technique), what's required to make it work (frame-accurate seeking problems, HEVC/VP9 alpha, requestVideoFrameCallback), and the image-sequence alternative (Apple AirPods-style canvas drawImage of a JPEG/WebP sequence): bytes cost, decode cost, and the modern alternative of a single sprite sheet. Also cover the simplest premium option: a pre-rendered aurora ribbon PNG/WebP set moved with CSS transforms on a scroll timeline.

6. Also research: `prefers-reduced-motion` handling best practice for background ambient motion specifically (what WCAG 2.3.3 / the reduced-motion guidance actually says, and what real sites do — do they freeze, reduce amplitude, or swap to a static frame?). Find real code-pattern guidance from MDN / web.dev / a11y writeups.

7. Also check: is `content-visibility`, `will-change`, or compositing-layer advice relevant? And what about the hero above-the-fold LCP cost of each approach?

Give a RECOMMENDATION: best premium result without shipping a heavy 3D runtime, for a company that ALREADY OWNS real rendered aurora ribbon art assets (PNGs). Consider a layered-parallax approach with real art + CSS scroll timelines + a cheap noise/grain layer.

Cite real URLs (MDN, web.dev, caniuse, Chrome Developers blog, bundlephobia, real articles). Return findings DIRECTLY in your final message. Do NOT write .md files. Do not write code beyond tiny inline snippets if essential. Target ~700-900 words, dense and specific.

## WCAG 2.3.3 and `prefers-reduced-motion`

WCAG 2.3.3 (Animation from Interactions, Level AAA) states: "Motion animation triggered by interaction can be disabled, unless the animation is essential to the functionality or the information being conveyed."

## Implementation Best Practices

Web content should ideally respect user preferences using CSS media queries (`@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`), as this is often the most elegant and user-friendly solution, allowing users to set their preference once at the OS level.

For 'triggered by interaction' animations, motion must happen because the user did something — scrolled, clicked, hovered, dragged — where the user's action did not inherently require that motion. ## Key Techniques and Approaches

**Canvas Frame Sequence Method:**
The most reliable approach extracts video clips to individual frames at a specific framerate, then draws them onto a canvas using GSAP's ScrollTrigger to map scroll progress to frame indices. A canvas frame sequence has every frame already decoded and ready, so there is no seek delay, and whatever speed a visitor scrolls at, the image keeps pace exactly, providing precision as the entire point of the technique.

**requestVideoFrameCallback:**
FrameScrub syncs seeks to actually painted frames via requestVideoFrameCallback, not just animation timing, so it never visibly stutters or jumps ahead. The HTMLVideoElement.requestVideoFrameCallback() method allows web authors to register a callback that runs when a new video frame is sent to the compositor, allowing developers to perform efficient per-video-frame operations such as painting to a canvas.

**Why Direct Video Seeking Falls Short:**
Scroll-scrubbing a video element is unreliable: seeking is async, keyframe intervals cause visible stutter, and mobile Safari fights you on autoplay and inline playback. Unfortunately, the video element does not guarantee frame-accurate seeking.

**Canvas drawImage Approach:**
Canvas frame-swapping has no seek lag: the frame is already decoded, so drawing it is immediate, making this superior to trying to scrub video elements directly.

This Apple-style technique has become popular for premium portfolio animations and product demonstrations precisely because the deterministic frame mapping prevents the stuttering and jank inherent in traditional video seeking.

## Key Findings

**will-change and Compositing Overhead:**
Permanent `will-change` declarations can harm performance since modern browsers already promote actively-animating elements to the compositor when needed, and removing them reduces compositing cost without visual animation differences. `will-change` should be an exception, not part of every component's default CSS.

**Proper Usage of will-change:**
Only use `will-change` on elements that animate continuously (backgrounds, looping effects) or are about to animate (add class on hover, remove after transition). Each promoted layer consumes GPU memory, and on pages with many animated elements this can cause memory pressure and slow things down.

**Hero Animations and LCP Impact:**
An LCP candidate must be visible on the first paint; if it starts at opacity: 0, the browser ignores it and delays LCP. Starting at opacity: 0.1 is nearly invisible to humans but fully visible to Core Web Vitals measurement. If a hero section has a full-screen video or canvas animation, the LCP element can be delayed while the animation initializes.

**Compositing Layer Best Practices:**
Stick to transform and opacity changes for animations, promote moving elements with `will-change` or `translateZ`, but avoid overusing promotion rules since layers require memory and management.

**Background Images and LCP:**
The preload scanner reads markup, not CSS, so background images are discovered late, while an Image widget outputs a normal image tag that the preload scanner sees immediately and can start downloading early.

## Memory and Performance Constraints

A decoded frame at full resolution occupies width × height × 4 bytes, so buffering an image sequence at 1080p consumes memory quickly and will be terminated by mobile browsers. Reducing resolution is usually the honest fix — a scroll-driven sequence is typically small on screen and rarely needs full resolution.

## Image Sequence vs. Video Approaches

The alternative approach is an image sequence: pre-extract frames as individual images and swap them on scroll. This is completely reliable and gives exact frame control, but downloading hundreds of images is expensive, so it suits short sequences at modest resolution.

## Sprite Sheet Benefits

Converting each frame to WebP resulted in a total combined size of 1.7MB, but packing all of those into a WebP spritesheet image brings the size down further to 1.5MB. That's a relatively modest 10% improvement, but still significant especially at scale. We're able to load all of the frames for the animation in a single network request, so concerns about HTTP/1 request bottlenecks are significantly lessened.

## Decoding Performance

The most expensive operation is image decoding. Decoding is necessary operation that takes compressed .jpg or .png and decode it to a bitmap. Modern APIs like createImageBitmap() and background decoding can help, but browser support and memory usage must be handled carefully.

## WebP for Animations

WebP takes less time to decode in the presence of seeking. In these scenarios, animated WebP takes 0.57x as much total decode time as GIF, resulting in less jank during scrolling and faster recovery from CPU utilization spikes.

## Pattern Overview

The pattern uses @supports for progressive enhancement — the effect should be decorative, not essential. For broader browser support, wrap them in @supports and let the animations be a progressive enhancement.

## How It Works

The recommended progressive enhancement pattern starts with base styles where no animation and content is always visible, then applies scroll animation only if supported inside the @supports block. Here's the structure:

1. **Base State**: Define your element's default, visible appearance
2. **Feature Detection**: Wrap scroll-driven animations in `@supports (animation-timeline: scroll())` or `@supports (animation-timeline: view())`
3. **Enhanced State**: Apply animations only for supporting browsers

## Why This Pattern Works

Because animation-timeline is simply ignored by browsers that don't understand it, fallbacks are straightforward — the animation just won't play and the element will be in its final state or its default state.

Chrome and Edge have supported scroll()/view() timelines unflagged since Chrome 115 (July 2023); Safari shipped support in Safari 26 (September 2025). Firefox still sits behind a layout.css.scroll-driven-animations.enabled flag, despite being a named Interop 2026 priority.

## Key Advantage

# Compositor-Only Properties and Layer Management

## Compositor-Only Properties

Only two CSS properties can be animated by the compositor without triggering layout or paint: **`transform`** and **`opacity`**. These represent the most performant animation approach.

## Guidance on will-change and Layer Promotion

To promote elements onto their own compositor layer, use:

```css
.moving-element {
  will-change: transform;
}
```

For older browsers, apply `transform: translateZ(0)` instead.

## Critical Warnings

**On avoiding excessive promotion:**

> "Every layer you create requires memory and management, and that's not free."

The article emphasizes that on memory-constrained devices, the performance cost of unnecessary layers can outweigh any benefits.

**Direct warning against blanket promotion:**

> "Do not promote elements unnecessarily."

The article specifically discourages applying `will-change: transform` and `transform: translateZ(0)` to all elements (`*` selector), as this creates excessive layers requiring GPU texture uploads and bandwidth allocation.

## Performance Target

Aim for approximately **4-5ms** spent in compositing during performance-critical actions like scrolling or transitions. Use Chrome DevTools' layer profiler to monitor layer counts and identify why layers were created.
